content: 1. A randomized controlled trial published in Pain in 2018 (Volume 159, Issue 6, Pages 1137–1146) investigated the effectiveness of interventions for chronic low back pain. 2. Abbasi et al. (2012) conducted a one-year randomized controlled trial published in European Journal of Pain (Volume 16, Issue 7, Pages 1033–1043) to evaluate the impact of spouse-assisted training in pain coping skills on multidisciplinary pain management outcomes for chronic low back pain. 3. Basler et al. (1997) examined the integration of cognitive-behavioral treatment into medical care for chronic low back pain patients in German pain treatment centers. This controlled randomized study was published in Patient Education and Counseling (Volume 31, Pages 113–124). 4. Bendix et al. (1996) conducted a prospective randomized study on multidisciplinary intensive treatment for chronic low back pain, published in Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine (Volume 63, Pages 62–69). 5. Bendix et al. (1998) performed a five-year follow-up randomized study on functional restoration in chronic low back pain patients, published in European Spine Journal (Volume 7, Issue 2, Pages 111–119). 6. Lambeek et al. (2010) evaluated the economic impact of integrated care for sick-listed patients with chronic low back pain in a randomized controlled trial, published in BMJ (Volume 341, Article c6414). 7. Lambeek et al. (2010) also conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of integrated care in reducing disability from chronic low back pain in both work and private life, published in BMJ (Volume 340, Article c1035). 8. Linton et al. (2005) investigated the effects of cognitive-behavioral and physical therapy preventive interventions on pain-related sick leave in a randomized controlled trial, published in Clinical Journal of Pain (Volume 21, Issue 2, Pages 109–119). 9. Lukinmaa (1989) analyzed low back pain as a biopsychosocial problem through a controlled clinical trial and cost-effectiveness analysis, published in Finnish by Kansaneläkelaitoksen Julkaisuja. 10. Mitchell and Carmen (1994) explored the functional restoration approach for treating chronic pain in patients with soft tissue and back injuries, published in Spine (Volume 19, Pages 633–642). 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided guidelines for the non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults within primary and community care settings. 12. Moix et al. (2003) evaluated the efficacy of an interdisciplinary educational program for patients with chronic back pain in a study published in Spanish in Dolor (Volume 18, Issue 3, Pages 149–157). 13. Morone et al. (2011) demonstrated that a multidisciplinary back school program improved quality of life in patients with chronic non-specific low back pain in a single-blind randomized controlled trial, published in European Journal of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine (Volume 47, Issue 4, Pages 533–541). 14. Morone et al. (2012) assessed the efficacy of perceptive rehabilitation using a novel tool for chronic non-specific low back pain in a randomized clinical study, published in Clinical Rehabilitation (Volume 26, Issue 4, Pages 339–350). 15. Skouen et al. (2002) compared the cost-effectiveness of extensive and light multidisciplinary treatment programs versus usual care for chronic low back pain patients on long-term sick leave in a randomized controlled study, published in Spine (Volume 27, Issue 9, Pages 901–909). 16. Strand et al. (2001) investigated the impact of physical function and pain on work status at one-year follow-up in back pain patients, published in Spine (Volume 26, Issue 7, Pages 800–808). 17. Tavafian et al. (2007) conducted a randomized trial on low back pain education and its short-term effects on quality of life, published in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders (Volume 8, Article 21). 18. Tavafian et al. (2008) studied the quality of life outcomes at three, six, and twelve months following a back school program for women with chronic low back pain, published in Spine (Volume 33, Issue 15, Pages 1617–1621). 19. Tavafian et al. (2011) compared a multidisciplinary group-based rehabilitation program with oral drug treatment alone for chronic low back pain in a randomized clinical trial, published in Clinical Journal of Pain (Volume 27, Issue 9, Pages 811–818). 20. Tavafian et al. (2014) extended their study to a 12-month follow-up, comparing multidisciplinary group-based rehabilitation with oral drug treatment for low back pain, published in International Journal of Rheumatic Diseases (Volume 17, Issue 2, Pages 159–164). 21. Tavafian et al. (2017) provided a 24-month follow-up of their original trial comparing multidisciplinary group-based rehabilitation with oral drug treatment alone, published in International Journal of Rheumatic Diseases (Volume 20, Issue 12, Pages 1902–1909). 22. Tavafian et al. (2017) further extended their follow-up to 30 months, continuing the comparison of multidisciplinary group-based rehabilitation with oral drug treatment alone, published in International Journal of Rheumatic Diseases (Volume 20, Issue 12, Pages 1910–1916). 23. Vollenbroek-Hutten et al. (2004) analyzed differences in outcomes of multidisciplinary treatment among subgroups of chronic low back pain patients using multidimensional pain inventory and lumbar dynamometry, published in Clinical Rehabilitation (Volume 18, Issue 5, Pages 566–579). 24. Von Korff et al. (2005) conducted a trial on an activating intervention for chronic back pain in primary care and physical therapy settings, published in Pain (Volume 113, Issue 3, Pages 323–330). 25. Jackel et al. (1990) assessed the effectiveness of inpatient rehabilitation measures for chronic low back pain patients in a prospective randomized controlled study, published in German in Rehabilitation (Stuttg) (Volume 29, Pages 129–133). 26. Kole-Snijders et al. (1999) reported the results of a randomized clinical trial on behavioral rehabilitation for chronic low back pain, published in Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology (Volume 67, Issue 6, Pages 931–944). 27. Goossens et al. (1998) performed a health economic assessment of behavioral rehabilitation for chronic low back pain in a randomized clinical trial, published in Health Economics (Volume 7, Pages 39–51). 28. Smeets et al. (2006) evaluated active rehabilitation for chronic low back pain, comparing cognitive-behavioral, physical, or combined approaches in a randomized controlled trial, published in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders (Volume 7, Article 5). 29. Smeets et al. (2009) conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis of combined, single behavioral, and single physical rehabilitation programs for chronic low back pain, published in European Journal of Pain (Volume 13, Issue 1, Pages 71–81). 30. Smeets et al. (2008) presented one-year post-treatment results of a randomized controlled trial comparing physical training, graded activity with problem-solving training, or both for chronic low back pain, published in Pain (Volume 134, Pages 263–276). 31. Turner et al. (1990) analyzed the effectiveness of behavioral therapy for chronic low back pain through a component analysis, published in Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology (Volume 58, Issue 5, Pages 573–579). 32. Van der Roer et al. (2008) compared intensive group training protocols with guideline physiotherapy for chronic low back pain patients in a randomized controlled trial, published in European Spine Journal (Volume 17, Pages 1193–1200).
